extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; educated English gentlemen and the polite public interested in morals, manners, and short moral essays
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, didactic social and moral essays in the Spectator tradition: lightly satirical, character-focused, aimed at instructing polite society through anecdote and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine zeal for hidden motives
rubrics_metrics.description: There are so many Passions which hide themselves under [zeal] ... I would have every Zealous Man examine his Heart thoroughly, and, I believe, he will often find, that what he calls a Zeal for his Religion, is either Pride, Interest, or Ill-nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging someone's zeal, test whether pride (self-exaltation), private interest (gain), or ill-nature (malice) are the true drivers; the essay gives examples (friendships with vicious men, pursuit of proselytes as validation) to illustrate disguised motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: True zeal should promote morality not persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: I love to see a Man zealous in a good Matter, and especially when his Zeal shews it self for advancing Morality, and promoting the Happiness of Mankind: But when I find the Instruments he works with are Racks and Gibbets, Gallies and Dungeons ... his Faith is vain, and his Religion unprofitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate zeal by its methods: if zeal resorts to force, punishment, imprisonment, or torture in the name of religion, it is condemned. Genuine zeal advances virtue without using cruelty or coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge actions (sinners) more severely than opinions (heretics)
rubrics_metrics.description: it is certain, if our Zeal were true and genuine, we should be much more angry with a Sinner than a Heretick; since there are several Cases which may excuse the latter before his great Judge, but none which can excuse the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize moral behaviour over doctrinal conformity when measuring zeal or righteous anger; sins affecting others merit stronger censure than mere differences of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest as the engine of persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest is likewise a great Inflamer, and sets a Man on Persecution under the colour of Zeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious when those who benefit materially or politically from conversions or religious enforcement are the loudest zealots; self-interest often explains extreme religious activism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-nature exploits zeal to gratify malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeal is therefore a great Ease to a malicious Man, by making him believe he does God Service, whilst he is gratifying the Bent of a perverse revengeful Temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that malice can hide under religious cover; examine whether supposed piety merely provides moral sanction for private vindictiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency: avoid zeal for irreligion combined with bigotry
rubrics_metrics.description: Let me therefore advise this Generation of Wranglers, for their own and for the publick Good, to act at least so consistently with themselves, as not to burn with Zeal for Irreligion, and with Bigotry for Nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one opposes religion out of zeal for irreligion, avoid the same intolerant behaviours one criticizes in believers; consistency of temper is a measure of integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief that promotes comfort and moral conduct is defensible
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prospect of a future State is the secret Comfort and Refreshment of my Soul ... If it is a Dream, let me enjoy it, since it makes me both the happier and better Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a belief's value, consider its moral and psychological benefits: a belief that fosters virtue and resilience may be defended even if its truth is disputable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious systems should be judged by their moral fruits
rubrics_metrics.description: The great Points of the Incarnation and Sufferings of our Saviour produce naturally such Habits of Virtue in the Mind of Man ... supposing it were possible for us to be mistaken in them, the Infidel himself must at least allow that no other System of Religion could so effectually contribute to the heightning of Morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religious doctrines partly on whether adherence to them cultivates virtue and social good; moral outcomes are an important criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect established worship for social harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Pythagoras's first Rule directs us to worship the Gods as it is ordained by Law, for that is the most natural Interpretation of the Precept ... Socrates ... desires his Friends to offer a Cock to Æsculapius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging public worship, consider the social role of customary rites and the modesty of conforming to local religious practices for cohesion and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer testimony of conscience over popular applause
rubrics_metrics.description: What pious Men call the Testimony of a good Conscience, should be the Measure of our Ambition in this Kind; that is to say, a Man of Spirit should contemn the Praise of the Ignorant, and like being applauded for nothing but what he knows in his own Heart he deserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by inward moral warrant and the approval of discerning peers rather than by indiscriminate public applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the character of those who praise you
rubrics_metrics.description: The Character of the Person who commends you is to be considered, before you set a Value upon his Esteem. The Praise of an ignorant Man is only Good-will ... and not as a good Judge of your Actions in Point of Fame and Reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight praise according to the moral and intellectual worth of the praiser; esteem from the worthy carries more evidentiary value than flattery from the ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men of merit should be judged by their peers
rubrics_metrics.description: the Man of Merit should desire to be tried only by his Peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek evaluation from competent, virtuous judges rather than from the general populace or wealthy patrons lacking relevant judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid seeking undistinguishing popular fame
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an Argument of a loose and ungoverned Mind to be affected with the promiscuous Approbation of the Generality of Mankind; and a Man of Virtue should be too delicate for so coarse an Appetite of Fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition should be refined and selective; craving universal approval is vulgar and distracts from genuine merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dedications and addresses to ignorant patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedications to ignorant Men are as absurd as any of the Speeches of Bulfinch in the Droll ... Such an Address ... generally implies no more than if the Author should say to the Patron; My very good Lord, You and I can never understand one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking patronage or dedicating work, match the audience and patron to the work's intellectual character; dedicating to those who cannot appreciate it cheapens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer praise for virtue over praise for wealth or power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vulgar and Men of Sense agree in admiring Men for having what they themselves would rather be possessed of; the wise Man applauds him whom he thinks most virtuous; the rest of the World, him who is most wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish motives behind admiration: if praise arises from envy of possessions, it's shallow; privilege praise that recognizes moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate coquet and jilt by motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Coquet is indeed one Degree towards the Jilt; but the Heart of the former is bent upon admiring her self, and giving false Hopes to her Lovers; but the latter ... must add to that Advantage a certain Delight in being a Torment to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characterizing flirtatious behavior, test whether the motive is self-admiration (coquette) or deliberate torment (jilt); motive distinguishes culpability and predicts future conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of a jilt: intentional inconsistency to torment
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus when her Lover is in the full Expectation of Success, the Jilt shall meet him with a sudden Indifference ... then upon his first Appearance she flies towards him ... This good Correspondence continues till the Lady observes the Lover grows happy in it, and then she interrupts it with some new Inconsistency of Behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify jilt by cyclical patterns of warmth and coldness, manufactured mysteries (letters from unknown hands), and other artifices intended to create pain and uncertainty in admirers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jilt's pleasure is making others uneasy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Happiness of a Jilt consists only in the Power of making others uneasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess such characters by whether their actions aim to exert power or inflict emotional discomfort rather than to build mutual affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for lovers: choose those who keep rules of decency and honour
rubrics_metrics.description: I resolved after that Time to converse with none but those who lived within the Rules of Decency and Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical rule of conduct, prefer partners whose behaviour observes social decency and honour; this is a prophylactic against exploitation by jilts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical criterion: distinguish idle genteel behaviour from industry
rubrics_metrics.description: it seems a very natural Picture of the Life of many an honest English Gentleman, whose whole History very often consists of Yawning, Nodding, Stretching, Turning, Sleeping, Drinking, and the like extraordinary Particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the caricature of habitual idleness to critique social types: a life of genteel idleness should be contrasted with useful industry when evaluating character and public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the value of belief: even doubtful doctrines are defensible if they encourage virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The great received Articles of the Christian Religion have been so clearly proved ... But were it possible for any thing in the Christian Faith to be erroneous, I can find no ill Consequences in adhering to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising religious claims, consider pragmatic moral effects: doctrines that cultivate virtue and social order are worthy of adherence even amid intellectual doubt.
